chapters.title: Chapter 5: Using History Without Being Fooled by It

lessons.title: Valuations Through the Cycle: Nifty PE at Tops and Bottoms

body.text: Valuation is a terrible timing tool and an excellent expectations tool. It will not tell you what the Nifty does next month. It has told you, far more often than not, whether the next five years are likely to be generous or disappointing.

children.text: Every chapter of this course kept returning to one idea from Lesson 1.1: price equals earnings multiplied by the P/E ratio, and swings in the P/E drive most of the cycle. The Nifty Fifty in 1972, Japan in 1989, the Sensex in 1992 and 2008 all ended with investors paying extreme multiples. Chapter 5 turns that history into practical tools, starting with the most useful one: where is the market's valuation compared with its own past, and what has that meant for the returns that followed?
The Nifty's P/E at Tops and Bottoms

body.title: Nifty 50 trailing P/E at major turning points (approximate)

children.text: Line the chart up against Chapter 3. The deepest bottoms, 2003 and October 2008, came with P/Es around 11 to 12. The big tops, January 2008, late 2010, early 2018 and late 2021, came with P/Es in the mid to high 20s. Most of the time the Nifty has traded somewhere between the high teens and mid 20s. The range itself shifts slowly over time as interest rates, the index's sector mix and India's growth prospects change, so compare today's figure with the last ten to fifteen years rather than with a single magic number.

body.text: Two traps when reading Nifty P/E history. First, from April 2021 NSE switched the Nifty's P/E calculation from standalone to consolidated company earnings, which lowered the reported P/E, so figures before and after that date are not strictly comparable. Second, the P/E can spike when earnings collapse, not because prices are high: the standalone P/E rose to around 40 in early 2021 because COVID had crushed the previous year's profits. Always ask whether a high P/E comes from high prices or from temporarily low earnings.

body.title: Read the P/E Correctly
body.question: In early 2021, the Nifty's standalone trailing P/E hit around 40, far above its 2008 peak of about 28, yet the index went on to rise for most of that year. What best explains this?
options: The market was in a far bigger bubble than in 2008 and a crash was certain
Trailing earnings had collapsed temporarily during COVID, so the P/E looked extreme even though prices were not, and earnings then recovered strongly
NSE had made an error in the index calculation
P/E ratios have no relationship with earnings
body.explanation: A trailing P/E divides today's price by the last twelve months of earnings. When earnings drop sharply for a temporary reason, the P/E jumps even if prices are reasonable. As profits recovered in 2021, the P/E fell back while prices rose. This is the same effect as the cyclical P/E paradox from Lesson 4.1, applied to the whole index.

children.text: What Starting Valuation Has Meant for the Next Five Years

body.title: Annual Nifty price return over the next five years, by starting point

children.text: The pattern is clear, and so are its limits. Starting from P/Es in the low teens produced exceptional five-year returns. Starting from the high 20s produced poor to modest ones. But the relationship is loose: January 2018, at a P/E of about 27, still delivered around 10% a year because earnings recovered strongly after COVID, while December 2011, at a P/E of 17, produced less than March 2020 at the same P/E. Six data points are a teaching example, not proof. Longer studies of Indian and global markets show the same broad tendency, with plenty of exceptions.

body.label: The price of buying at the top
body.value: Nifty at a P/E of ~28 in January 2008: roughly zero price return over five years
body.context: India's economy and corporate earnings grew substantially between 2008 and 2013. Investors who started at the peak valuation saw almost none of that growth in the index level, because the P/E had to fall back first.

children.text: Over any period, the return from an index comes from three sources: growth in earnings, the change in the P/E, and the dividends paid along the way. The first and third are driven by the economy and companies. The second is driven by the cycle, and it is the only one whose direction you can reasonably judge in advance, because a P/E that starts very high has more room to fall than to rise.

body.caption: g = annual earnings growth, n = number of years. An approximation, but a useful one.

body.title: Great Earnings, Poor Returns
body.prompt: Nifty earnings grow at a strong 12% a year for 5 years, but the P/E falls from 28 to 18 over the same period. Ignoring dividends, what is the approximate annual price return? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: P/E factor over 5 years = 18 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.643. Annualised, that is 0.643 to the power 1/5 ≈ 0.915, meaning the falling multiple subtracts roughly 8.5% a year. Annual return ≈ 1.12 × 0.915 − 1 ≈ 2.5%. Earnings growth of 12% a year delivered only about 2.5% a year in price, very close to what actually happened to investors who bought in January 2008.

body.caption: Common market valuation measures, and what to watch out for

cells: Price relative to the last twelve months of earnings
Distorted when earnings are temporarily very high or very low
Price relative to analysts' estimates of next year's earnings
Estimates are usually too optimistic at tops and too pessimistic at bottoms
Price relative to the net assets on company balance sheets
Less meaningful for asset-light businesses like IT and consumer brands
Cash returned to shareholders as a share of price
Indian dividend payouts are low and vary, so the signal is noisy
Total listed market value relative to the size of the economy
Rises structurally as more companies list and the economy formalises
Whether shares look cheap or expensive relative to safe bonds, from Lessons 1.3 and 4.2
The normal gap changes with growth expectations and risk appetite

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: From April 2021, NSE began calculating the Nifty's P/E using ___ earnings instead of standalone earnings.
body.explanation: Consolidated earnings include profits of subsidiaries, which better reflect large groups' true earnings. The change lowered the reported P/E, so when comparing today's Nifty P/E with 2008 or 2018, remember the two series are not measured the same way.

columns.label: Valuations are good for
points: Setting realistic expectations for the next five to ten years
Deciding whether to lean slightly more or less into equities within your planned range
Spotting extremes, such as P/Es near 28 or near 11
Resisting euphoria and panic with an objective number
Choosing how gradually to deploy a large lump sum

columns.label: Valuations are bad for
points: Predicting next month's or next year's direction
Calling exact tops and bottoms: expensive markets can get more expensive for years
Justifying stopping SIPs completely and waiting in cash
Comparing across eras without adjusting for rates, sector mix and methodology
Replacing a financial plan based on your own goals

body.title: A Twice-a-Year Valuation Check
steps: Download the Nifty 50 P/E, P/B and dividend yield from niftyindices.com
Compare the current P/E with its range over the last ten to fifteen years, remembering the 2021 methodology change
Check whether earnings are unusually high or low right now, which can distort the P/E
Compare the Nifty's earnings yield with the 10-year G-sec yield
If valuations are near an extreme, consider adjusting your equity allocation modestly within a pre-decided range, not all at once
Write down what you decided and why, so your future self can check it against what happened

body.title: The Inheritance and the Expensive Market
body.scenario: It is late September 2024. The Nifty is at a record high with a P/E around 24, near the top of its recent range. Your friend in Bengaluru has just inherited ₹30 lakh and has a long-term goal 15 years away. She also runs a ₹20,000 monthly SIP. Her brother tells her to stop the SIP and keep all ₹30 lakh in a fixed deposit until the P/E falls to 16.
body.prompt: Using this lesson, what would a sensible, valuation-aware approach look like?
body.modelAnswer: Her brother is right that valuation matters: a P/E near the top of the range has historically been followed by more modest returns than a P/E near the bottom, so expecting another 2003 or 2020 would be unrealistic. But his plan turns an expectations tool into a timing rule. The Nifty might not return to a P/E of 16 for many years, and expensive markets can stay expensive while earnings grow into the valuation, as happened after January 2018. Stopping the SIP is also the wrong lever: SIPs spread purchases across many valuations, including future cheaper ones, which is exactly what a long-term investor wants. A more balanced approach is to keep the SIP running, decide a long-term target allocation for the inheritance, perhaps a mix of equity and debt suited to a 15-year goal, and deploy the equity portion gradually, for example through a systematic transfer plan from a debt or liquid fund over 12 to 24 months, rather than as one lump sum at a record high. If valuations fall sharply during that period, she can accelerate within her plan. In fact the Nifty fell about 17% over the next six months, which a staggered approach would have partly used to her advantage, although nobody could have known that in advance.

The total value of listed companies divided by the size of the economy. A broad valuation gauge that rises structurally as more companies list.

Moving a lump sum from a debt or liquid fund into an equity fund in regular instalments, spreading purchases across different market levels.

children.text: Every time valuations reached an extreme in this course, someone had a convincing argument for why the old ranges no longer applied. Lesson 5.2 examines the most expensive words in investing, "this time is different", and the rare occasions when they turned out to be true.

body.text: P/E figures, index levels and returns in this lesson are approximate, rounded, before dividends, and based on a small number of illustrative dates. They are not a forecast, and past relationships between valuation and returns may not hold in future. Nothing here is investment advice. Consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for decisions about your own money.

points: Nifty P/Es around 11 to 12 marked the deep bottoms of 2003 and 2008, while P/Es in the mid to high 20s marked the tops of 2008, 2010, 2018 and 2021
Starting valuation has been a useful guide to five-year returns: about 40% a year from a P/E of 12 in 2003, about 0% from a P/E of 28 in January 2008, with many exceptions in between
Returns come from earnings growth, change in P/E and dividends, so 12% earnings growth with the P/E falling from 28 to 18 gives only about 2.5% a year
Watch for distortions: the April 2021 switch to consolidated earnings, and P/E spikes when earnings temporarily collapse
Use a dashboard of measures, not one number, and compare each with its own recent history
Valuations are for setting expectations and making modest allocation tilts, not for stopping SIPs or timing tops and bottoms
